circles.name: Limbo
circles.description: Nothing here is wrong on purpose. Encodings drifted, spaces crept in, a BOM rode along. These rows are not sinners, they are the unbaptised: they never got a chance to be correct. All of it is repairable.

rules.title: Mojibake from a latin-1 export read as UTF-8
rules.rationale: The accounting export is latin-1. Read as UTF-8 it yields "VanackerÂ ", "KortrÃ¯jk". The mapping is lossless and reversible, so the engine fixes it and logs the original bytes.

rules.title: Non-breaking spaces and zero-width characters
rules.rationale: U+00A0 and U+200B survive every trim() a user tries. They break joins silently because the strings look identical on screen.

rules.title: Leading, trailing and doubled whitespace
rules.rationale: Cosmetic in the source and join-breaking in the target. A trailing space is invisible in every spreadsheet and decisive in every lookup, so two records that read identically on screen refuse to match on load.

rules.title: Byte order mark on the first column header
rules.rationale: A BOM makes the first column unaddressable by name, which usually surfaces as a missing mandatory field rather than as an encoding issue.

rules.title: Entity codes in mixed case and with inner spaces
rules.rationale: "san-0098", "SAN 0098" and "SAN-0098" are one article. Codes are case-folded and space-stripped before any matching happens.

circles.name: Lust
circles.sin: The same customer, five times over
circles.description: Four sources, no shared key. Every sales rep kept their own list, so "Vanacker BVBA", "Vanacker b.v.b.a." and "VANACKER" are one company with three credit limits. Matching is cheap; deciding which record survives is not.

rules.title: Near-duplicate customers above the auto-merge threshold
rules.rationale: Blocking on postcode plus normalised name, scored with token_set_ratio. At or above 92 the pair is the same legal entity in every sample we reviewed, so the engine merges and records the losing record.

rules.title: Near-duplicate customers in the grey band
rules.rationale: Between 80 and 92 the score cannot separate "Bouwbedrijf Deveux" from "Bouwbedrijf Deveux Zonen", which are a parent and its subsidiary with separate credit limits. A wrong merge destroys a credit history, so sales decides.

rules.title: Survivorship conflict on merge
rules.rationale: When two matched records disagree on payment terms or credit limit, completeness cannot pick a winner. Merging on "most complete record" would silently raise a credit limit.

rules.title: Identical VAT number on records with different names
rules.rationale: A shared VAT number is strong evidence of one entity, but it is also how a trading name and its legal entity appear. Finance owns the call.

circles.name: Gluttony
circles.description: A single column holding a street, a box number, a postcode, a VAT number and two email addresses. The legacy system had no field for it, so the users made one.

rules.title: Postcode and city embedded in the street field
rules.rationale: Belgian postcodes are four digits in a known range and appear in a fixed position relative to the city name, which makes the split deterministic.

rules.title: Box number inside the house number
rules.rationale: "12 bus 3", "12/3" and "12 b3" are one house number and one box. The target ERP has separate fields and rejects the combined value.

rules.title: Multiple email addresses in one cell
rules.rationale: Split on the usual separators, first address becomes primary, the rest become additional contacts. Order is preserved because the first address is the one the users have been mailing.

rules.title: Unparseable address soup
rules.rationale: "achter de kerk, bellen bij de poort" is a real delivery instruction and not an address. Guessing a street here invents data.

rules.title: VAT number hidden in the company name
rules.rationale: Users with no VAT field typed it into the name. Extracting it recovers a mandatory field, and the pattern is unambiguous.

circles.name: Greed
circles.sin: Money that will not say what it means
circles.description: Comma or dot, euro or franc-era text, VAT in or VAT out, discount baked into the unit price. Every one of these is a cent that lands in the wrong ledger.

rules.title: Decimal comma, dot or both as thousand separator
rules.rationale: "1.247,50", "1,247.50" and "1247.5" are the same amount. The engine uses the separator order within the string, never locale guessing.

rules.title: Amounts stored as text with currency symbols
rules.rationale: "€ 1.247,50", "EUR 1247,50" and "1247,50 euro" are one amount written by three people. The currency text carries no information here, because the whole ledger is in euro, so stripping it loses nothing and makes the column numeric.

rules.title: Ambiguous VAT treatment on a price
rules.rationale: The price file has an "incl" column that is populated for 61 percent of rows and contradicted by the article VAT rate for some of them. A wrong reading moves 21 percent of a sales price. Finance decides per row.

rules.title: Discount baked into the unit price
rules.rationale: Where the unit price is below cost and a discount agreement exists for the same article, the discount was almost certainly applied twice. The engine flags the pair instead of unwinding it.

rules.title: Negative or zero unit price on a sellable article
rules.rationale: A sellable article with a price of zero or less cannot be migrated: the target ERP will create order lines from it on day one.

circles.name: Wrath
circles.sin: Sources at war with each other
circles.description: The same article is sold per piece in one file, per box in another and per metre in a third. No file is wrong on its own. Together they cannot all be true.

rules.title: Conflicting unit of measure across sources
rules.rationale: Piece, box and metre for one article differ by a factor of 50 in stock value. Source precedence cannot settle it because the warehouse file is the most accurate and the least authoritative.

rules.title: Conflicting article description across sources
rules.rationale: Descriptions are not load-critical. The engine takes the master file and keeps the alternatives as a note, so nothing is lost and nobody is asked.

rules.title: Conflicting primary supplier for one article
rules.rationale: Purchasing drives replenishment from this field. A wrong supplier places real orders.

circles.name: Heresy
circles.sin: Values that pass every format check and are still false
circles.description: BE0000000000 is a structurally valid VAT number. 1900-01-01 is a valid date. noreply@noreply.be is a valid address. These rows pass validation and poison the ERP, which is exactly what makes them heretics: they look like believers.

rules.title: Structurally valid but placeholder VAT number
rules.rationale: BE0000000000 and BE9999999999 satisfy the modulo check and identify nobody. Migrating them produces invoices that cannot be reported.

rules.title: Sentinel dates standing in for "unknown"
rules.rationale: 1900-01-01, 1899-12-30 and 9999-12-31 are the legacy system's way of saying null. They become null, which is what they always meant.

rules.title: Placeholder contact details
rules.rationale: noreply@, geen@geen.be, phone 000000000 and "/" are absence written as presence. Nulling them is honest; keeping them sends mail to nowhere.

rules.title: Test and scratch records left in the master file
rules.rationale: "TEST", "ZZZ OUD - NIET GEBRUIKEN", "KLANT NIEUW" and "aaa" are working notes. They have order history, which is why nobody ever dared delete them.

rules.title: Country code outside ISO 3166-1 alpha-2
rules.rationale: "XX", "B" and "BELG" are each recoverable, but "B" is also a legacy code for Belgium and a valid code for nothing. Low volume, so ask.

circles.name: Violence
circles.sin: What Excel did to the data on its way here
circles.description: Article codes turned into 1.23E+11. Leading zeros eaten off an EAN. Dates silently converted to serial numbers, or worse, to a US reading that is also a valid European one. The user never touched these cells.

rules.title: Article code converted to scientific notation
rules.rationale: 1.23E+11 lost its trailing digits when Excel stored it as a float. The value cannot be recovered from the cell, only from a second source, so the engine pairs it with the master file and asks for confirmation.

rules.title: Leading zero stripped from an EAN
rules.rationale: An EAN is fixed length and carries a check digit, so left-padding it back is verifiable rather than assumed, which is what separates this from a guess. The same damage cannot reach a Belgian postcode, because those run from 1000 to 9999 and have no leading zero to lose — so this rule covers articles only, rather than claiming a reach it does not have.

rules.title: Date stored as an Excel serial number
rules.rationale: 45291 is 2023-12-27. Deterministic, given the 1900 epoch and the leap-year bug.

rules.title: Date ambiguous between US and European reading
rules.rationale: "03/04/2024" is 3 April and 4 March. Both are plausible due dates and the difference decides whether an invoice is overdue. Guessing here is how an aging report starts lying.

rules.title: Numeric field containing a formula error
rules.rationale: #REF!, #N/B and #DIV/0! are not values. The cell never held one.

circles.name: Fraud
circles.sin: References to things that do not exist
circles.description: Discount agreements for customers that were deleted in 2019. Articles assigned to a supplier that went bankrupt. Open items for a customer number that is not in any master file. The keys look fine. They point at nothing.

rules.title: Discount agreement for a customer that does not exist
rules.rationale: An orphan agreement cannot be migrated and would otherwise be silently dropped by the loader, which is worse than rejecting it loudly.

rules.title: Article pointing at a supplier that is not in the master
rules.rationale: The article is real and sellable. Only its replenishment link is broken, so rejecting the article would be an overreaction.

rules.title: Open item for an unknown customer number
rules.rationale: An open receivable without a customer cannot be migrated, and it must be reported rather than dropped because it is money owed.

rules.title: Active article sourced from a blocked supplier
rules.rationale: The reference is intact and the data is consistent. The business fact is the problem, and only purchasing can decide whether to reroute or block.

circles.name: Treachery
circles.sin: The data that is clean, loads fine and is still wrong
circles.description: The deepest circle is reserved for betrayal. A migration that balances to zero because two errors cancel each other out will pass a net-total reconciliation, load without a single warning, and be discovered by the accountant in March. Only component-level reconciliation catches it.

rules.title: Row count reconciliation per entity
rules.rationale: Every source row must end in exactly one of Paradiso, Purgatorio or Inferno.

rules.title: Open receivables reconcile to the cent
rules.rationale: The sum of migrated plus held plus rejected open items must equal the source total exactly. Cents are not a rounding concern here, they are the test that nothing was invented or lost.

rules.title: Compensating errors detected by gross movement
rules.rationale: This is the ninth circle. A net total of zero difference can hide a pair of equal and opposite errors, so the gate also compares the sum of absolute per-customer differences. Net zero with gross movement is betrayal, not balance, and it fails the run.

rules.title: No customer may lose its entire open balance
rules.rationale: A customer whose source balance is non-zero and whose migrated balance is zero is the single most expensive migration defect: it is invisible in totals and discovered when the customer stops paying.
